title: OpenAI's release of mathematical findings draws concerns from experts
key_facts: OpenAI released over 370 mathematical results on Tuesday (6 Oct 2026), across algebra, theoretical computer science and mathematical logic.
The Guardian says that last month OpenAI solved the Navier-Stokes equation, one of the world's toughest mathematical problems, with a $1m reward for a solution.
The Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, an independent group of mathematical experts, said it does not endorse testing the most advanced problems on proprietary AI models.
The Institute's statement says AI can now output mathematical arguments that the prompting human cannot understand, verify or take responsibility for.

Tristan Buckmaster, a New York University mathematician who was working on the Navier-Stokes problem, told the New York Times that mathematicians prompting the models may have supplied information that helped the model reach its result.
OpenAI said it would work with the Institute for Advanced Study to give mathematicians a voice, but did not say it would stop testing its models on these problems.
The advisory board asked AI labs to grant the global mathematics community equitable access to their models.
quote_evidence: It is now the case that AI can output mathematical arguments in situations without the human who prompted it being able to understand the arguments, verify them, or take responsibility for them.
There's likely to be a bunch of results where they take someone's work and then take it to completion.
The use of proprietary internal models by AI labs to do mathematical research risks creating a two-tier system where labs outrun the rest of the field.
why_it_matters_hint: Mathematicians question whether results from proprietary AI models can be checked and credited, and whether the wider field can get access to the same tools.
